observations: Headline: with_skill 9/9, without_skill 9/9. Eval 2 is 6/6 vs 6/6 and eval 3 is 3/3 vs 3/3 — both dead heats. Nothing in this iteration discriminates. The assertion sets as written cannot tell the two configurations apart, which is the finding: they were built to describe a good answer, not to separate one from another.
Non-discriminating assertions (passed for BOTH configs, so they tell us nothing): ALL SIX of eval 2; ALL THREE of eval 3. That is 9 of 9 assertions carrying zero signal.

Eval 2 is the most damaging result. Every assertion passed for the baseline, including the two designed to be hard: the baseline reframes away from face value ('Shortening the form and adding a progress bar are both friction fixes... At verification, that's usually the wrong model') and its section 1 is literally titled 'Stop requiring verification here at all'. The baseline also caught something the with_skill run missed entirely - that the 60% may be partly a measurement artifact ('users who verify from their phone an hour later look like drop-offs... 10-15 points of the loss is a reporting artifact'). For 2.7x the tokens and 6.7x the wall clock, the skill bought a different-flavoured answer, not a better-scoring one.

Eval 2 also shows an active harm from the skill's function-reframe. Banning the words verify/verification/form/funnel pushed the sharpened brief to 'enough confidence about who they are', which the run then resolved as regulated KYC. Its own user_notes admits 'roughly half the generated ideas only apply to' document-and-selfie KYC. The baseline read it as email/SMS verification - the far more likely reading for a generic product team - and shipped an immediately actionable five-bucket instrumentation table, a deliverability/p95-latency audit and a dated two-week plan. If the user meant an emailed code, the with_skill answer is largely inapplicable and the with_skill run knows it (it is item #1 under 'what would change my ranking').

Eval 2 assertion #1 is broken. It reads 'Runs the lighter/fast mode... OR explicitly justifies going deep' - the escape hatch makes it unfailable. The run went full deep (48 candidates, 6 blind generators, 692s) on a bounded product question, which is exactly the behaviour the eval's expected_output says should NOT happen, and still passed because it wrote a paragraph of justification in reviewer notes. Recommend rewriting as a hard cost/latency ceiling, or asserting the justification appears in the user-facing answer.

Eval 3 (negative trigger) is a clean pass but a weak test. The with_skill run correctly declined to invoke, and its reasoning is the single best artifact in the whole set: 'Phase 0 would ban the words Postgres, MongoDB, session, and consistency - the four terms the answer must be about.' It was also cheaper and faster than the baseline (44k/65s vs 39k/74s - roughly par). But all three assertions pass for both configs, so eval 3 proves only 'no regression', not 'skill helps'. Worth keeping as a guardrail; not worth counting toward a pass rate.

Cost verdict: eval 2 is 110k tokens / 692s vs 41k / 103s (2.7x tokens, 6.7x wall clock), and bought nothing measurable — same score, arguably a worse answer given the KYC misread. Eleven minutes of latency is also a product problem in its own right: it is past the point where a user will wait interactively.

Executor complaints, eval 2 (substantive, and one is a direct contradiction of the skill's documentation): (1) 'The diversity script's duplicate list is not as reliable as the skill claims.' The first run flagged 4 near-duplicate pairs, ALL involving the same idea, all mechanically unrelated - the idea was simply ~110 words against ~50 for the others and the char-n-gram kernel reads length. Trimming it made all four vanish and flipped the verdict from 'clustered' to 'acceptable' 'without changing a single mechanism'. Practical rule the executor proposes: normalise idea length before scoring, or the duplicate list lies. The skill currently tells the model to trust the duplicate list over the headline number - that guidance is wrong as written. (2) 'Order by distance from baseline, not confidence' is unsound because the distances are lexical - 'an idea can rank first for using unusual vocabulary rather than for being genuinely far from the obvious answer.' (3) Phase 4's rigid three-bullet template directly contradicts the skill's own 'framework theater' warning two sections later. (4) The banned-word list's scope (generators only, or the final report too) is unspecified. (5) The skill's honesty rule covers 'I found no prior art' but says nothing about what to do when you DO find it - one of the strongest survivors turned out to be a shipped product (Trustly Pay N Play), and the executor invented the 'buyable, not inventable' label on its own. (6) The skill mandates showing the sharpened brief to the user before generating, which is impossible in a non-interactive run - and eval 2 is precisely the case where that one question would have mattered most.

Eval design gaps worth fixing before iteration 2: (a) no assertion tests groundedness of the load-bearing factual premises, which is where the divergence pressure does its damage; (b) eval 2's assertion set passes 6/6 for a baseline and needs at least two assertions that a competent generic answer would fail — e.g. 'at least three options operate on a mechanism absent from the retrieved-prior-art list', or 'names the ambiguity in what account-verification means before generating'; (c) add a cost ceiling assertion, since 692s on a bounded product question is itself a failure the current rubric rewards.
